# Windows Explorer Order

A small C/C++ library for Windows that, given a file path, finds an Explorer window open at that file's directory and returns a list of the files **in the order Explorer is displaying them**, plus the index of the given file in that list.

The intended purpose is to inform applications which file should be opened next (or previously) to follow the current display order of the explorer window they were opened from.

*Generated by Claude Opus 5.5 as a <u>proof of concept</u>.*

```c
ExplorerFileList *list = ExplorerOrder_GetFiles(L"C:/images/test.jpg");
if (list) {
    for (size_t i = 0; i < list->count; ++i)
        wprintf(L"%ls\n", list->paths[i]);      /* full paths, in on-screen order */
    /* list->index is test.jpg's position in paths, or -1 if it isn't listed */
    ExplorerOrder_Free(list);
}
/* NULL: no open Explorer window shows that folder */
```

Files: `explorer_order.h` (API), `explorer_order.cpp` (implementation, ~390 lines), `example.c` (command-line demo).

Link with: `ole32.lib shell32.lib shlwapi.lib oleaut32.lib uuid.lib user32.lib mpr.lib`

## How it works

1. The requested path is resolved to its full path, and both the file and its folder are passed through the Windows shell's own parser. This gives them exactly the form Explorer uses to report its windows and items, so short (8.3) names, forward slashes and long paths need no special handling.
2. Open Explorer windows come from the shell's window list (`ShellWindows`); the desktop is included as one more candidate. For each window, Windows reports the folder it shows (`IShellBrowser` → `IShellView` → `IFolderView`).
3. Windows showing the requested folder are matched by file system path, with mapped drives converted to their network form. If several match, the most recently active one is chosen, based on the order windows are stacked on screen and, on Windows 11, which tab is selected.
4. The chosen window's items are requested in display order (`IFolderView::Items` with `SVGIO_FLAG_VIEWORDER`), 128 at a time. Folders are skipped using file attributes stored in each item, which needs no disk access. The rest are turned into full paths.
5. The result is returned as an array of paths, plus the index of the requested file.

All Windows interfaces used exist on Windows XP. A newer comparison function (Vista+) is used when present.

## What has been considered and confirmed

Items marked *(by design)* follow from how the code works but were not specifically tested; see "Tests performed" for what was.

### Features

- Accepts any path to a file; the file itself does not need to exist (only its folder is used to find the window).
- Accepts forward slashes, relative paths, any capitalization, 8.3 short names and paths longer than 260 characters.
- Returns full paths of files only: subfolders are excluded, and their contents are never read.
- .zip files and shortcuts (.lnk, .url) count as files, even though Explorer can open them like folders.
- Hidden files are returned only if Explorer is showing them.
- Order follows the window's sort (any column, either direction, including Explorer's natural number sort, e.g. "55 …" before "1984 …") and grouping.
- Files in collapsed groups are included, in their normal position (by design).
- `index` gives the requested file's position in the list, or -1 if it isn't listed (doesn't exist, is a folder, or is hidden in that window).
- Returns `NULL` when no window shows the folder (including when the folder doesn't exist).
- An open window on a folder with no files returns a list with `count == 0` (distinguishable from `NULL`) *(by design)*.
- Several windows or tabs on the same folder: the most recently active is used (frontmost window; within a window, the selected tab).
- Windows 11 tabs are supported: the selected tab is preferred over other tabs in the same window *(by design; no two-tab test, as tabs can't be opened from code)*.
- The real desktop is supported: for a file on the Desktop with no window showing the Desktop folder, the desktop's icons are listed in on-screen order (down each column, then across). A window showing the Desktop folder takes priority *(by design)*.
- Mapped drives (`M:\…`) and network paths (`\\server\share\…`) to the same folder match.
- Other routes to the same folder, such as `Desktop\Folder` vs `C:\Users\Name\Desktop\Folder`, or a folder opened through a library, should match, since windows are compared by file system path *(by design)*.
- Works with network shares and OneDrive folders; cloud-only (not downloaded) OneDrive files are listed without being downloaded.
- Works with windows open inside a .zip file (including subfolders of the zip). The returned paths (e.g. `C:\a\photos.zip\one.jpg`) are shell paths, not real files: normal file functions such as `CreateFile` or `fopen` can't open them.
- Plain C interface, callable from C and C++; `EXPLORER_ORDER_API` macro for building or using as a DLL.
- One function to call and one to free; all memory is allocated with `CoTaskMemAlloc` and freed by `ExplorerOrder_Free`.
- Initializes COM itself if the calling thread hasn't, and also works if the caller already uses single-threaded or multithreaded COM *(only the uninitialized case was tested)*.
- No global state, so it can be called from several threads *(by design)*.

### Compatibility

- Targets Windows XP through Windows 11, on x86, x64, ARM64 and 32-bit ARM.
- Only functions available on Windows XP are imported (verified from the compiled import table). `CompareStringOrdinal` (Vista+) is looked up at run time; XP falls back to an invariant-locale comparison.
- Compiled with the Windows headers restricted to the XP API level, so anything newer fails to compile.
- Written in C++98, with no standard library, no exceptions and no C runtime memory functions. `example.c` is C89.
- 32-bit programs work with 64-bit Explorer.
- An x86 build also runs on ARM64 Windows through Windows' built-in emulation.
- Building for XP needs an XP-capable toolset (Visual Studio 2017/2019 `v141_xp`, Visual Studio 2008/2010, or MinGW); current Visual Studio cannot produce XP-compatible programs.
- 32-bit ARM needs Visual Studio 2022's ARM tools (Visual Studio 18 removed 32-bit ARM); with clang-cl, compile 32-bit ARM with exceptions off (`/EHs-c-`) because clang crashes on that target otherwise.
- 32-bit ARM programs run on Windows 10 on ARM and Windows 11 before 24H2; Windows RT does not allow third-party desktop programs.
- Earlier separate Windows 7+, Vista and XP versions were merged into this single version after confirming the XP-compatible code loses nothing on newer Windows.

### Tests performed (Windows 11, x64 and x86 builds unless noted)

- Order matches Explorer for: name A→Z, name Z→A, date modified (newest first), and grouped by type in both directions (grouped order checked against what Explorer shows via Windows' accessibility interface).
- Changing a window's sort and re-running changes the result to match.
- Two windows on the same folder with different sorts: bringing each to the front in turn switches the result each time.
- Path forms: forward slashes with uppercase name, 8.3 short name, a 290-character file path, a missing file (-1), a folder (-1), a folder with no window (`NULL`).
- File types: .txt, .zip, a shortcut to a folder (all included); a subfolder and a folder named like a file (excluded).
- Windows showing the Desktop folder, a drive root (`C:\`), the real desktop with no windows open (auto-arrange off; order follows icon positions).
- 5,000-file folder with 200 subfolders.
- A window still loading (5,000 local files; network share): polled from the moment the window opened; results were always `NULL` (window not yet registered) or the complete list, never partial.
- Network share (515 files): all 514 visible files in Explorer's exact natural name order; the missing one is the hidden `Thumbs.db`.
- Mapped drive vs network path: window opened either way, path passed either way: all match.
- OneDrive folder with 27 cloud-only photos: order matches Explorer; all 27 still cloud-only afterwards.
- A filtered window (`*.png`): Explorer turns it into "Search Results", so the folder isn't matched and `NULL` is returned.
- A window open inside a .zip file (sorted Z→A): files returned in the window's order with the subfolder excluded; a file in a subfolder of the zip; a missing file inside the zip (-1); the zip file's own path with no window on its folder (`NULL`). Also run with the forced XP code paths.
- Collapsed group: files still returned (as intended).
- The XP-only code paths (item-by-item reading and the invariant-locale comparison) forced on and run on Windows 11: same results.
- Builds: MSVC x86 and x64 at warning level 4 with no warnings; clang `-Wall -Wextra` with only a harmless padding warning; ARM64 and 32-bit ARM compiled with clang-cl (not run).
- C++98 compliance checked with clang (`-Wc++98-compat-pedantic`), and the check itself was confirmed to catch a planted C++11 feature; `example.c` checked as strict C89.

### Performance

- 5,200 items: 485 ms originally, about 59 ms now (about 8× faster), including starting the example program.
- Gains came from fetching items in batches instead of one call per item, reading file/folder status from the item data instead of the disk (saves a network round trip per file on shares), and only checking window recency for matching windows.
- Batch sizes 64, 128 and 256 were compared (61, 59 and 57 ms median): 128 was kept, as larger sizes were within measurement noise.
- The XP fallback path reads items one at a time and is slower (about 1.5 s for 5,200 items on Windows 11); it only runs if a view rejects the display-order request.

### Security review

- No memory-safety problems found: buffer sizes come from Windows and are checked, every string is terminated, every allocation is freed exactly once on all paths, and list growth cannot overflow before memory runs out.
- No `LoadLibrary`; the one run-time lookup uses kernel32, which is always loaded, so DLL planting isn't possible through this code.
- Untrusted input paths could make Windows contact other computers (e.g. `\\host\share` sending login credentials) or parse archive files inside the program. Not applicable here: the calling program fully controls the paths.
- Programs running as administrator or as a service would process data from other user programs and load shell components; not applicable to this project.
- Calls into Explorer have no time limit, so a hung Explorer window can block the caller; judged not an issue for this project (calling from a background thread avoids it).
- `example.c` uses fixed format strings; Windows file names can't contain control characters, so no terminal escape issues.

### Simplification

- Hand-written path conversion (short/long names, long paths) was replaced by the shell's own parser.
- Hand-written helpers replaced by Windows functions: `PathFindFileNameW`, `SHStrDupW`, `CoTaskMemAlloc` (removing string copies), `WNetGetUniversalNameW`, `SHGetDataFromIDListW`.
- Considered and rejected: `IShellWindows::FindWindowSW` for matching (returns one window, not the most recent, and misses other routes to the same folder); ATL `CComPtr` or `_com_ptr_t` (not available with all XP-era compilers; the latter throws exceptions); comctl32 dynamic arrays and `SHBindToObject` (extra dependency, or not available by name on XP).

### Shortcomings and untested areas

- Only Windows 11 (build 26300, x64) has run the code. XP, Vista, 7, 8.x and 10 have not been tested, nor has ARM hardware.
- Not built with an actual XP-era compiler or older Windows SDK headers; C++98 compliance was checked with a modern compiler.
- XP: grouping ("Show in Groups") is not reflected in the order; whether XP accepts the display-order request is unknown (it falls back to item-by-item reading); finding the real desktop may not work (it then behaves as if there were no desktop).
- XP folder windows with auto-arrange off: the order is Explorer's internal order, not the icon positions. (Windows 7+ folder windows can't turn auto-arrange off; the desktop can, and is handled.)
- XP has no exact character-by-character name comparison; names differing only by invisible characters (e.g. soft hyphens) could compare equal there.
- Filtered or searched windows return `NULL`, because Explorer turns them into search results.
- Paths returned for a window inside a .zip file can't be opened with normal file functions; the calling program must use the shell (e.g. `SHCreateItemFromParsingName`) or extract them first.
- The same server reached by two different names (IP address vs host name) is not recognized as the same folder.
- A folder reached through a symbolic link or junction is not matched to its target (not tested).
- Only File Explorer windows are found; other file managers are not.
- "Most recently active" is based on window stacking order: a window that was just minimized moves behind others. When neither of two duplicate tabs is selected, the choice between them follows the tab windows' stacking order, which hasn't been confirmed to track tab switching.
- For the first fraction of a second after a window opens (0.25–0.7 s in tests) it isn't registered yet, so the call returns `NULL`.
- In case-sensitive folders, two files whose names differ only in case: `index` points to the first.
- Items without a file system path (e.g. "This PC" on the desktop) are not returned.
- Folders whose own path is over 260 characters can't be opened by Explorer, so they never match (confirmed).
- Programs running elevated may not see Explorer's windows at all (not tested; not relevant to this project).
